items.content:
Big Boys On My Roof™ — Growing up, Anthony Stockdale struggled with his love for bigger men. His new photo series celebrates the bear community.

I came out as gay when I was young, but for a long time it felt like I still had another secret to explain. I wasn’t just attracted to men. I was attracted to big men, hairy men, older men, bellies, beards, thick arms; the sort of bodies I never saw presented as desirable in the gay culture available to me growing up in North East England – or even anywhere visible on the internet, TV, film – anywhere whatsoever. 

For years, I didn’t even know there was a word for it. I had no idea what a “bear” was, never mind that there was an entire culture built around men who looked like the ones I was drawn to. So even after coming out as gay, I still felt slightly alien within gayness itself. I’d done the frightening bit and told people I liked men, only to realise I then had to explain why the men I liked looked nothing like the ones I was apparently supposed to fancy. 

Essentially, I had to come out twice. 

Back then, I did a lot of bleak teenage mental maths. If I was gay already, and then only attracted to this very particular kind of man, surely I had reduced the number of people I might ever meet to about 0.000001% of the population. It genuinely felt that scarce. 

  • Read next: The raw, fledgling intimacy of Peter Hujar’s contact sheets

At 35, the whole thing has flipped. While some of my friends are beginning to panic about getting older, losing their hair or moving further away from whatever version of youth they once associated with desirability, I find myself heading in the opposite direction. People within the bear community often find themselves entering their prime at an older age. “The Daddy Era.”

More importantly, I eventually discovered that bears are everywhere. London, Berlin, Madrid, Rome. Bars, clubs, beaches, festivals, on the train, in the corner shop. What once felt like some impossibly niche defect in my sexuality turned out to be a whole international community. 

The men around me now are friends, lovers, exes, dates, people I’ve met through nightlife, people I’ve travelled with, people I argue with, laugh with and care about. They are not an abstract category of body that I happen to fancy. They have populated my life. 

That is what Big Boys On My Roof™is about. 

The photo series started completely by accident. In the summer of 2023, my flatmate and co-dog dad was bringing me a drink through the rooftop hatch of our flat in Soho. I looked down and saw his head and shoulders framed by this enormous square opening and thought it looked sick. I took a picture on my phone. That was it. 

  • Read next: Jesse Glazzard’s messy portrait of queer friends, lovers and chosen family

But I kept coming back to it. There was something funny and intimate about this huge man emerging through a tiny domestic opening, but there was also something about the way the hatch framed him. It also felt like it was starting to speak to a particular point I’ve reached in my life. It turned this completely ordinary part of my home into a little portrait studio. The picture felt affectionate without trying to announce itself as affectionate. 

So I started doing it again. Whenever one of these men happened to be at my flat, I photographed them coming through the same hatch. Same place, same framing device, different man. There was no casting brief and no attempt to decide who was or wasn’t sufficiently “bear” to qualify. They are simply men who exist in my life. 

That repetition became important to me. The hatch gives everyone the same stage, but each person occupies it differently. Their faces, bodies, clothes, expressions and personalities do the rest. Some images are funny, some are tender, some are sexy, some slightly awkward. I like that. I never wanted the series to feel like a catalogue of a body type. 

Because bigger queer men are still strangely under-celebrated as they are. Gay culture has become much more expansive in the ways it talks about sexuality, gender and masculinity, but body representation can still feel remarkably narrow. Bigger men are everywhere in queer life, yet much less visible in the images that are used to represent it. When they do appear, their size can become the entire point of the image, rather than simply one part of who they are. 

  • Read next: The suave style and subtle codes of gay San Francisco in the ’70s

I wanted to photograph these men without asking them to symbolise anything. No transformations. No before-and-after narrative. No argument about what a bear should weigh, wear or look like. Just portraits of men I think are beautiful, made in the place where my life with many of them actually happens. 

That has also changed the way I think about getting older as a gay man. Ageing is often talked about as a process of losing something: youth, desirability, attention. My experience has been almost the reverse. Getting older has brought me closer to myself and deeper into a community I spent my teenage years believing barely existed. 

What once made me feel isolated is now one of the things that gives me the strongest sense of belonging. That is the shift I wanted the photographs to hold: from scarcity to abundance, from imagining there was something wrong with what I wanted to understanding that there are many different standards of beauty, attraction and intimacy. 

The men I once calculated made up approximately 0.000001% of the population are everywhere in my life now. 

Sometimes they literally come through my roof.

Anthony Stockdale is a freelance writer.

items.title_es: Retratos de osos gay a través de una escotilla en la azotea
items.content_es:
Grandes chicos en mi techoTM — Creciendo, Anthony Stockdale luchó con su amor por los hombres más grandes. Su nueva serie de fotos celebra la comunidad de osos.

Salí como gay cuando era joven, pero durante mucho tiempo se sentía como si todavía tuviera otro secreto que explicar. No sólo me sentía atraído por los hombres. Me sentía atraído por hombres grandes, hombres peludos, hombres mayores, barbas, brazos gruesos; el tipo de cuerpos que nunca vi presentado como deseable en la cultura gay disponible para mí creciendo en North East England – o incluso en cualquier lugar visible en Internet, TV, película - en cualquier lugar.

Durante años, ni siquiera sabía que había una palabra para ello. No tenía ni idea de lo que era un “bear”, no importaba que hubiera un completo cultura Construí alrededor de los hombres que parecían los que yo estaba dibujado. Así que incluso después de salir como gay, todavía me sentía un poco alienígena dentro de la homosexualidad misma. Yo había hecho la parte aterradora y le dije a la gente que me gustaban los hombres, sólo para darme cuenta de que entonces tenía que explicar por qué los hombres que me gustaban no parecían a los que aparentemente se suponía que me gustaban.

Esencialmente, tuve que salir dos veces.

En ese entonces, hice muchas matemáticas mentales adolescentes desoladas. Si yo era gay ya, y entonces sólo quedaba a este tipo muy particular de hombre, seguramente había reducido el número de personas a las que podría conocer alrededor del 0.000001% de la población.

  • Lea el siguiente: La intimidad cruda y persistente de las hojas de contactos de Peter Hujar

A los 35 años, todo ha volteado. Mientras algunos de mis amigos están llegando a entrar en pánico por envejecer, perder el pelo o alejarse más lejos de cualquier versión de la juventud que alguna vez se asocian con la conveniencia, me encuentro en la dirección opuesta. La gente de la comunidad de osos a menudo se encuentra entrando en su primer momento en una edad mayor. “La Era de papá”.

Más importante aún, eventualmente descubrí que los osos están en todas partes. Londres, Berlín, Madrid, Roma. Bares, clubes, playas, festivales, en el tren, en la tienda de esquina. Lo que una vez se sentía como un defecto imposiblemente nicho en mi sexualidad resultó ser una comunidad internacional entera.

Los hombres que me rodean ahora son amigos, amantes, exes, fechas, personas que he conocido a través de la vida nocturna, personas con las que viajado, personas con las que discuto, risa con y cuidar. no son una categoría abstracta de cuerpo que me sucede a la fantasía. Ellos han poblado mi vida.

Eso es lo queBig Boys On My Roof™Se trata de eso.

En el verano de 2023, mi compañero de piso y mi padre co-dog me llevaba una copa por la escotilla de la azotea de nuestro apartamento en Soho. Miré hacia abajo y vi su cabeza y hombros enmarcados por esta enorme abertura cuadrada y pensé que parecía enfermar. Tomé una foto en mi teléfono. Eso fue todo.

  • Lea el siguiente: Jesse Glazzard es un retrato desordenado de amigos queer, amantes y familia elegida

Pero yo seguía reviviendo a ello. Había algo gracioso e acerca de este enorme hombre emergendo a través de una pequeña apertura doméstica, pero también había algo sobre la forma en que la escotilla lo enmarcaba. También podíamos decir a un punto en particular que él alcanzó en mi vida. Convirtió esta parte completamente ordinaria de mi casa en un pequeño estudio de retrato. La imagen se encuentra afectuosa sin tratar de anunciarse a sí misma como cariñosa.

Así que empezamos a hacerlo de nuevo. Cada vez que uno de estos hombres estaba en mi piso, los fotografié a través de la misma escotilla. El mismo lugar, el mismo dispositivo de encuadre, el hombre diferente. No había un casting breve y ningún intento de decidir quién era o no era suficiente "sorecer" para calificar. Ellos son simplemente hombres que existen en mi vida.

Esa repetición se hizo importante para mí. La escotilla da a todos la misma etapa, pero cada persona la ocupa de manera diferente. Sus caras, cuerpos, ropa, expresiones y personalidades hacen el resto. Algunas imágenes son divertidas, son tiernas, algunas son sexys, algunas son sexys, algo inusual incómodas. Me gusta. Nunca seguir que la serie se sintiera como un catálogo de un tipo de cuerpo.

Debido a que los hombres más grandes aún son extrañamente sub-celebrados como son. La cultura gay se ha vuelto mucho más expansiva en las formas en que habla de sexualidad, género y masculinidad, pero la representación del cuerpo todavía puede sentirse notablemente estrecha. Los hombres más grandes están en todas partes en la vida queer, pero mucho menos visible en las imágenes que se utilizan para representarlo. Cuando aparecen, su tamaño puede convertirse en el punto entero de la imagen, en lugar de simplemente una parte de quiénes son.

  • Lea el siguiente: El estilo suave y los códigos sutiles de gay San Francisco en los años 70

Quería fotografiar a estos hombres sin pedirles que evaran nada. No hay transformaciones. No hay narración antes y después. Ningún argumento sobre lo que un oso debe pesar, o parecer. Sólo retratos de hombres creo que son hermosos, hechos en el lugar donde mi vida con muchos de ellos realmente sucede.

Eso también ha cambiado la forma en que pienso en en envejecer como un hombre gay. El hábito se habla a menudo como un proceso de perder algo: juventud, conveniencia, atención. Mi experiencia ha sido casi el revés. Envejecer me ha acercado a mí mismo y más profundamente en una comunidad que llevaba mis años de adolescencia creyendo que apenas existía.

Lo que una vez me hizo sentir aislado es ahora una de las cosas que me da el sentido más fuerte de pertenencia. Ese es el cambio que quería que las fotografías se mantuvieron: de la escasez a la abundancia, de imaginar que había algo mal con lo que quería que hay muchos estándares diferentes de belleza, atracción e intimidad.

Los hombres que una vez cálculo representan aproximadamente 0.000001% de la población están en todas partes en mi vida ahora.

A veces, literalmente, vienen por mi techo.

Anthony Stockdale es escritor independiente.

items.title: In photos: Lives of solitude at the world’s edge
items.excerpt: Coirón — Pie Aerts’s new photobook documents years spent in close quarters with puesteros in Patagonia – a group of aging gauchos who live almost completely isolated existences. Pie Aerts first visited Patagonia in 201
items.content:
Coirón — Pie Aerts’s new photobook documents years spent in close quarters with puesteros in Patagonia – a group of aging gauchos who live almost completely isolated existences.

Pie Aerts first visited Patagonia in 2019. He had just quit his job in the Dutch corporate world, and along with his camera, Aerts travelled the entire length of the region, which stretches across Chile and Argentina at South America’s farthest tip. But among Patagonia’s vast expanses and dramatic peaks, he encountered a recurring figure who he couldn’t get out of his mind – the gaucho.

“They would emerge silently from the distance, almost like solitary silhouettes riding with cattle or alone,” Aerts remembers. “They intrigued me so I kept looking for them, but every time I found the courage to approach, they would disappear into the distance again.”

The photographer found himself particularly interested in a specific localised group of gauchos, puesteros, who live across the Greater Magallanes area at the very southernmost provinces of Patagonia. Named after their tiny workstations and homes – puestos – these often semi-nomadic animal herders and pastoralists commonly live and work without anyone else, managing huge private ranches that they do not own. Many had travelled from further north in Chile in search of work between the ’50s and ’70s while they were teenagers, and ended up staying to work as ranchers.

  • Read next: What life on the Strait of Hormuz is really like

In the 19th and 20th centuries, the area was one of the world’s most important wool factories. It saw a boom in sheep herding as the area was colonised, forcing the displacement of local indigenous people. The puesteros often herd hundreds of sheep, cows, horses and other livestock, while protecting them from poachers and other animals. On top of that, they manage the huge estates, or estancias, which have historically been owned by a very small handful of families. As the estancias grew aggressively in this period, it led to rural workers in the area become forced into low-wage work, with no ownership of the land they tend.

“Puesteros have traditionally been marginalised and suppressed,” Aerts explains. “On top of that, they have this long history of living in complete isolation, having spent decades in remote areas, largely separated from the outside world.”

Establishing contact with them proved difficult. With puesteros often keeping no company other than their horses and dogs for several months at at a time, most were reluctant to meet with someone from the outside world. “About three to four years into the project we got to a turning point, where I felt for the first time that they were not only accepting my presence, but embracing it in a way that they could feel it was sincere,” he says. “It was almost like a friendship after being with these guys for so many years.”

  • Read next: Guts, glory and goat tossing at the World Nomad Games

The result of his years-long persistence, along with the trust and friendship he built up with the puesteros, is his debut monograph Coirón, which is published by GOST. Featuring intimate shots taken inside their private quarters, it saw Aerts be given intimate access into their lives that few others have ever seen. It makes for an evocative portrait of a lifestyle that the wider world knows little about, while also provoking a thoughtful, existential meditation on the passing of time, ageing and how living alone almost completely removed from society can shape a person.

There are shots of the puesteros at work with their horses, close-ups of the interiors and ephemera they fill their downtime with, and dramatic landscape photographs of Patagonia’s wild emptiness. It’s a portrait of life that feels removed from time, yet completely attached to it. “There’s zero distraction, which makes it much easier to just exist in the current moment,” he says. “Many of these places are completely disconnected from the internet and any form of mobile reception. Once you live it with them, you follow the sequence of each day, which is extremely similar – almost every day is the same, but you get into this surreal, almost grounding rhythm in which you just live life.”

Throughot Coirón, the photographer brings to light their stories, which are often complex and layered. As the ranchers grow older, their bodies also slowly wane, and they slowly become incapable of doing the labour-intensive work that they have for decades. Some have wives and children, but the majority do not have a family.

  • Read next: The disappearing world of mountain farmers in the Alps

“So when you talk about these bigger human concepts such as ageing or retiring and the passage of time, you feel they exhibit at greater fear to retire than to die, because they are stuck in this lifestyle where there’s no provisions, no safety net and no social welfare system that catches them when they fall", Aerts continues. "So, when they are no longer able to do this backbreaking labour, no one is taking care of them.”

As such, many puesteros are hesitant to return to mainstream society when their bodies do eventually fail, where there is more infrastructure to support them. Some have small amounts of money in pension pots, but not all do. Though there are increasingly initiatives to provide them with retirement housing and care, spaces are extremely limited and can take several years to get one. 

“Many are forced to move into towns and cities without any plan,” Aerts adds. “We’ve been there when one of these gentlemen who had nothing in place went to pick up his life savings and to our complete surprise he just went straight onto a bar and started drinking it.”

  • Read next: Striking portraits of side-saddled, Mexican rodeo women in the USA

And among the stillness of the photos, lurking in the background is a changing Patagonia. It’s no longer the world’s main wool producing engine, and modernisation is creeping into the region, despite its remoteness. Tourism is increasingly one of rural Patagonia’s biggest areas of economic growth, which means that the majority of resources invested into the area is spent on conservation.

“It comes at the cost of these men,” says Aerts. “It comes at the cost of a culture that is not built for this disproportional influx in tourism – many young kids that come from the countryside move to the city, so it really is the last generation of puesteros. At this pace they are losing the gaucho culture that makes this region so special, because the focus is on protecting the national parks and wildlife too much. So my hope is that it rebalances into a willingness from the government to protect that cultural identity of the region.”

Being able to capture that culture up close is an important part of that mission, but what will stay the longest with Aerts is the friendships he made. “We had the most incredible experiences of just sitting through the coldest and windiest nights, just playing cards, getting drunk, talking about life with the cameras completely off,” he continues. “Sometimes we got stuck in that rhythm for a couple of days, in which we weren’t making a story anymore – we were just living.”

  • Read next: Exploring the impact of colonialism on Australia’s Indigenous communities

Coirón by Pie Aerts is published by GOST Books.

items.title_es: En fotos: Vidas de soledad en el borde del mundo
items.content_es:
Coirón — El nuevo fotolibro de Pie Aerts documenta años pasados en barrios cercanos con puesteros en la Patagonia, un grupo de gauchos envejecidos que viven existencias casi completamente aisladas.

Pie Aerts por primera vez visitó Patagonia en 2019. Acababa de dejar su trabajo en el mundo corporativo holandés, y junto con su cámara, Aerts viajó toda la extensión de la región, que se extiende a través de Chile y Argentina en la punta más lejana de Sudamérica. Pero entre las vastas extensiones y los picos dramáticos de la Patagonia, encontró una figura recurrente que no podía salir de su mente – el gaucho.

“Emerjan silenciosamente desde la distancia, casi como siluetas solitarias que andan con ganado o solos”, recuerda Aerts. “Me intrigaron así que los seguía buscando, pero cada vez que encontré el coraje de acercarse, ellos desaparecerían a la distancia de nuevo”.

El fotógrafo se encontró particularmente interesado en un grupo localizado específico de gauchos, puesteros, que viven a través de la zona de Magallanes Mayores en las provincias más meridionales de la Patagonia. Nombrado después de sus pequeñas estaciones de trabajo y hogares – puestos – estos a menudo semi-nómadas pastores animales y pastores comúnmente viven y trabajan sin nadie más, administrando enormes ranchos privados que no poseen. Muchos habían viajado desde el norte en Chile en busca de trabajo entre el ’50s y ’70Mientras eran adolescentes, y terminaron trabajando como rancheros.

  • Lea el siguiente: Lo que la vida en el Estrecho de Hormuz es realmente como

En los siglos XIX y XX, la zona era una de las fábricas de lana más importantes del mundo. Vio un boom en el pastoreo de ovejas mientras se colonizaba la zona, forcing the displacement of local indigenous gente. El puesteros a menudo se reparten cientos de ovejas, vacas, caballos y otros animales, mientras que protegen a los cazadores de caza furtivos y otros animales. estancias, que históricamente han sido propiedad de un puñado muy pequeño de familias. estancias Creció agresivamente en este período, lo que llevó a los trabajadores rurales de la zona a convertirse en trabajadores de bajos salarios, sin propiedad de la tierra que tienden.

“Puesteros tradicionalmente han sido marginados y suprimidos”, explica Aerts.Además de eso, tienen esta larga historia de vivir en aislamiento completo, habiendo pasado décadas en áreas remotas, en gran parte separadas del mundo exterior”.

Establecer contacto con ellos resultó difícil. puesteros a menudo no mantener ninguna compañía más que su horses y perros durante varios meses a la vez, la mayoría eran reacios a reunirse con alguien del mundo exterior. “Acerca de tres a cuatro años en el proyecto llegamos a un punto de inflexión, donde sentí por primera vez que no sólo aceptaban mi presencia, sino que lo abrazaban de una manera que podían sentir que era sincero”, dice. “Fue casi como una amistad después de estar con estos chicos durante tantos años”.

  • Lea el siguiente: Guts, gloria y cabras en los Juegos Nomad del Mundo

El resultado de su persistencia de años, junto con la confianza y la amistad que él construyó con la puesteros, es su monografía debut Coirón, que es publicado por GOST. Con imágenes íntimas tomadas dentro de sus cuartos privados, vio a Aerts tener acceso íntimo en sus vidas que pocos otros han visto jamás. Hace para un retrato evocador de un estilo de vida que el mundo más amplio conoce poco, mientras que también provoca una meditación meditada y existencial sobre el paso del tiempo, ageing y cómo vivir solo casi completamente alejado de la sociedad puede dar forma a una persona.

Hay disparos de los puesteros en el trabajo con sus caballos, acercamientos de los interiores y la esfímera que llenan su tiempo de inactividad, y dramáticas fotografías de paisaje del vacío salvaje de la Patagonia. Es un retrato de la vida que se siente alejado del tiempo, pero completamente unido a él. “Hay cero distracción, que hace mucho más fácil de existir en el momento actual”, dice. “Muchos de estos lugares están completamente desconectados. internet y cualquier forma de recepción móvil. Una vez que lo vives con ellos, sigues la secuencia de cada día, que es extremadamente similar – casi todos los días es el mismo, pero te metes en este ritmo surrealista, casi molido en el que sólo vives la vida.”

A través de Coirón, el fotógrafo trae a la luz sus historias, que a menudo son complejas y capas. A medida que los rancheros crecen, sus cuerpos también se van lentamente, y se vuelven lentamente incapaz de hacer el trabajo intensivo que tienen durante décadas. Algunos tienen esposas e hijos, pero la mayoría no tienen familia.

  • Lea el siguiente: El mundo desaparecido de los campesinos montañosos en los Alpes

“EntoncesCuando se habla de estos conceptos humanos más grandes como el envejecimiento o la jubilación y el paso del tiempo, se siente que exhiben un mayor temor a retirarse que a morir, porque están atrapados en este estilo de vida donde no hay disposiciones, ni red de seguridad y ningún sistema de bienestar social que los atrapa cuando caen", continúa Aerts. "Así, cuando ya no son capaces de hacer este trabajo desgarrador, nadie está cuidando de ellos".

Como tal, muchos puesteros son vacilantes de volver a la sociedad dominante cuando sus cuerpos fallan eventualmente, donde hay más infraestructura para apoyarlos. Algunos tienen pequeñas cantidades de dinero en ollas de pensiones, pero no todos lo hacen. Aunque hay cada vez más iniciativas para proporcionarles vivienda y cuidado de jubilación, los espacios son extremadamente limitados y pueden tomar varios años para conseguir uno.

“Muchos se ven obligados a mudarse a ciudades y ciudades sin ningún plan”, añade Aerts. “Hemos estado allí cuando uno de estos caballeros que no tenía nada en su lugar fue a recoger sus ahorros de vida y para nuestra completa sorpresa él acaba de ir directamente a un bar y empezó a beberlo”.

  • Lea el siguiente: Retratos de mujeres rodeo mexicanas de cara a cara en los EE.UU.

Y entre la quietud de las fotos, el acecho en el fondo es una cambiante Patagonia. Ya no es el motor principal de producción de lana del mundo, y la modernización se está arrastrando hacia la región, a pesar de su lejanía. Tourism es cada vez más una de las mayores áreas de crecimiento económico de la Patagonia rural, lo que significa que la mayoría de los recursos invertidos en la zona se gastan en conservación.

“Viene a costa de estos hombres”, dice Aerts. “Viene a costa de una cultura que no se construye para esta afluencia desproporcional en el turismo – muchos niños jóvenes que vienen del campo se mueven a la ciudad, por lo que realmente es la última generación de puesteros. A este ritmo están perdiendo la cultura gaucho que hace que esta región sea tan especial, porque el foco es proteger los parques nacionales y la fauna demasiado. Así que mi esperanza es que reequilibra la voluntad del gobierno para proteger la identidad cultural.

Ser capaz de capturar eso culture "Tuvimos las experiencias más increíbles de estar sentados a través de las noches más frías y con viento, jugando a las cartas, emborrachandose, hablando de la vida con las cámaras completamente fuera", continúa. "A veces nos quedamos atrapados en ese ritmo durante un par de días, en los que ya no estábamos haciendo una historia de vida", continuó. "A veces nos quedamos atrapados en ese ritmo durante un par de días.

  • Lea el siguiente: Explorando el impacto del colonialismo en las comunidades indígenas de Australia

Coirón de Pie Aerts es publicado por GOST Books.

items.excerpt: Hujar:Contact — A new photobook highlights the process of the legendary queer photographer, and his process of growing into the artist he ultimately became. Less than a year after Peter Hujar (1934–1987) learned he had
items.content:
Hujar:Contact — A new photobook highlights the process of the legendary queer photographer, and his process of growing into the artist he ultimately became.

Less than a year after Peter Hujar (1934–1987) learned he had AIDS, the photographer passed from the disease at the age of 53. In death, Hujar reemerged as one of the great visionaries of his generation, possessed with a devotion to art that remained beyond his years on Earth. Unlike his contemporary, Robert Mapplethorpe, who used notoriety to incendiary effect, Hujar preferred the slow burn of simple truths.

In his life, Hujar would produce just one book, Portraits in Life and Death, a sequence of just 41 photographs published in 1976. Few took notice, except those who saw Hujar from their extraordinary vantage point as his subjects. Half a century later, his intimate photographs of friends and lovers at the frontlines of New York’s radical underground including William S. Burroughs, David Wojnarowicz, Susan Sontag, John Waters, and Divine have become the standard bearer of contemporary portraiture. Hujar weaves images made in the Catacombs of Palermo throughout a book, a memento mori that takes on chilling effect as many pictured would succumb to AIDS. 

With the passage of time, the art world would discover what Hujar had always known: the camera was merely an instrument, no different than the pencil, paintbrush, or chisel. Although the hand of the artist has largely been overlooked in photography, the new exhibition and catalogue, Hujar: Contact, crafts a compelling case for the contact sheet as sketchbook, revealing the process in which the masterpiece emerges. More literally, Hujar marked the contact sheets with a red wax pencil, discreetly identifying those he wanted to print, leaving 5,783 photographs unseen until this moment. 

  • Read next: When David Wojnarowicz became Arthur Rimbaud

Curated by Joel Smith, who previously staged Peter Hujar: Speed of Life at the Morgan Library & Museum in 2018, Hujar: Contact is a passport into the past, inviting us to the world through the eyes of an artist devoted to the craft. “The contact sheet is the thing that endures. It is the seed that you planted,” says Smith. “As a photographer, you’re left with the material trace of what you did, and it might be the next evening or it might be years later that you make good on that and print something from that roll.” 

Where Henri Cartier-Bresson was seeking “the decisive moment,” Hujar was more often tasked with having to discern which of so many decisive moments was the story he wanted to tell. Consider his 1973 photograph of Candy Darling on Her Deathbed, a spellbinding portrait of the Warhol Superstar cast in the role of a lifetime. It is glamorous, enchanting, poignant, and heartbreaking in equal part, casting the viewer in a hypnotic reverie of what was and could never be. Cut to the contact sheet, and Candy Darling is cutting up with Jackie Curtis and Hujar, playing the part like Joan Crawford accepting Anne Bancroft’s Academy Award from her bed. 

Reading the contact sheets, one imagines Hujar as the filmmaker he dreamed of becoming in his youth. The sheets unfold like screen tests, the camera tracing the unspoken narratives. “Hujar wanted to make a picture about a whole person,” Smith says. “Cinematically, you can do that by telling a story and characterising the person by the things that happen and what they do about it. You get a much more concise version from the contact sheets, but it’s the same family of storytelling.” 

  • Read next: Jesse Glazzard’s messy portrait of queer friends, lovers and chosen family

But the story Hujar wanted to tell? Therein lies the rub, the delicate frisson that underlies the luminous silver of his photographs. “He was somebody who thought a lot about what a person is like and how they are liable to act in front of the camera,” Smith says. “The medium he worked in, in a sense, was provocation.” 

Hujar: Contact is on on view at the Morgan Library & Museum, New York, through October 25, 2026. The catalogue is published by MACK/Morgan Library & Museum, New York.

items.title_es: La intimidad cruda y persistente de las hojas de contactos de Peter Hujar
items.content_es:
Hujar:Contacto — Un nuevo fotolibro destaca el proceso del legendario fotógrafo queer, y su proceso de crecimiento en el artista que finalmente se convirtió.

Menos de un año despuésPeter Hujar (1934-1987) aprendió que tenía SIDA, el fotógrafo pasó de la enfermedad a la edad de 53. En la muerte, Hujar se reenergió como uno de los grandes visionarios de su generación, poseído con una devoción al arte que permanecía más allá de sus años en la Tierra. A diferencia de su contemporáneo,Robert Mapplethorpe, que usó notoriedad a efecto incendiario, Hujar prefirió la quemadura lenta de verdades simples.

En su vida, Hujar produciría sólo un libro, Retratos en Vida y Muerte, una secuencia de sólo 41 fotografías publicadas en 1976. Pocos tomaron nota, excepto aquellos que vieron a Hujar desde su punto de vista extraordinario como sus súbditos. Medio siglo más tarde, sus fotografías íntimas de amigos y amantes en las primeras líneas del metro radical de Nueva York, incluyendoWilliam S. Burroughs, David Wojnarowicz, Susan Sontag,John Waters, y Divino se han convertido en el portador estándar del retrato contemporáneo. Hujar teje imágenes hechas en las Catacumbas de Palermo a lo largo de un libro, memento morique toma el efecto escalofríos como muchos imaginados sucumbirían al SIDA.

Con el paso del tiempo, el mundo del arte descubriría lo que Hujar siempre había conocido: la cámara era simplemente un instrumento, no diferente al lápiz, pincel o cincel. Aunque la mano del artista se ha pasado por alto en gran medida en la fotografía, la nuevaexposición yCatálogo, Hujar: Contacto, elabora un caso convincente para la hoja de contactos como cuaderno de bocetos, revelando el proceso en el que emerge la obra maestra. Más literalmente, Hujar marcó las hojas de contactos con un lápiz de cera roja, identificando discretamente los que quería imprimir, dejando 5.783 fotografías invisibles hasta este momento.

  • Lea el siguiente: Cuando David Wojnarowicz se convirtió en Arthur Rimbaud

Curado por Joel Smith, que previamente se había escenificadoPeter Hujar: Velocidad de vida en el Museo de la Biblioteca Morgan en 2018, Hujar: Contactoes un pasaporte en el pasado, invitándonos al mundo a través de los ojos de un artista dedicado a la artesanía. “La hoja de contactos es la cosa que soporta. Es la semilla que plantaste,” dice Smith. “Como fotógrafo, te queda con el rastro material de lo que hiciste, y podría ser la próxima noche o podría ser años más tarde que haces bien en eso e imprimen algo de ese rollo.”

DondeHenri Cartier-Bresson estaba buscando “el momento decisivo”, Hujar se encargó más a menudo de tener que discernir cuál de tantos momentos decisivos era la historia que quería contar. Considerar su fotografía de 1973 Candy Darling en su lecho de muerteEs glamoroso, encantador, conmovedor y desgarrador en la misma parte, proyectando el espectador en un ambiente hipnótico de lo que era y nunca podría ser. Corta a la hoja de contactos, y Candy Darling está cortando con Jackie Curtis y Hujar, jugando la parte como Joan Crawford aceptando su Premio Annecro de la Academia Bancro.

Leyendo las hojas de contactos, uno imagina Hujar como el cineasta que soñó de convertirse en su juventud. Las hojas se desarrollan como pruebas de pantalla, la cámara que traza las narrativas no expresadas. “Hujar quería hacer una imagen sobre una persona entera”, dice Smith. “Cinemáticamente, usted puede hacer eso contando una historia y caracterizando a la persona por las cosas que suceden y lo que hacen al respecto.

  • Lea el siguiente: Jesse Glazzard es un retrato desordenado de amigos queer, amantes y familia elegida

Pero la historia que Hujar quería contar? En ella se encuentra el rubí, el aspecto frisón que subyace a la plata luminosa de sus fotografías. “Él era alguien que pensaba mucho sobre lo que una persona es y cómo son susceptibles de actuar frente a la cámara”, dice Smith. “El medio en el que trabajaba, en cierto sentido, fue provocación”.

Hujar: Contacto se encuentra en el Museo de la Biblioteca Morgan, Nueva York, hasta el 25 de octubre de 2026. El catálogo es publicado por MACK/Morgan Library & Museum, New York.

Miss Rosen es escritora independiente de artes y fotografía, síguela. X.

items.title: Jesse Glazzard’s messy portrait of queer friends, lovers and chosen family
items.excerpt: The Sound of Dirt and Beauty — The photographer’s debut monograph explores tender, unpolished moments shaped by the people who he surrounds himself with, while offering a window into the UK’s working-class LGBTQ+ community.
items.content:
The Sound of Dirt and Beauty — The photographer’s debut monograph explores tender, unpolished moments shaped by the people who he surrounds himself with, while offering a window into the UK’s working-class LGBTQ+ community.

Making a book is a complicated affair for Jesse Glazzard. 

Up until this point, the 32-year-old British photographer has existed in the world of self-published zines, fashioning visual records of his queer and trans circles: drag queens hoisting flamingo-candled cakes, performers encrusted in drying mud, lovers kissing against cherry-toned fabrics. Makeshift, inexpensive, and securely enclosed, Glazzard’s risograph tributes have largely passed through the hands of his friends and community, immune to commercial pressures. 

“With a zine, it’s a tenner, you know. I don’t want it to feel like I'm selling something. It just has its own life,” he says.

Enter The Sound of Dirt and Beauty, Glazzard’s debut monograph. It’s a warm-blooded and spiky invitation into his most intimate moments and his queer and working-class community: needles congested with testosterone, scabs and scars, taut binders, limbs reaching and grappling for tender embraces.

  • Read next: Defiant, sensuous portraits of the transmasc & non-binary community

“The goal was to make a book, but actually getting there – my God, I didn’t actually think it would happen. So there’s that feeling, and then there’s also wanting to protect the people in the imagery because the work is so personal,” says Glazzard.

A West Yorkshire native, Glazzard readily recognises his “underclassness”, describing his home environment as “grim bleakness”. This foundational element now informs his photography – grainy, murky, and largely black-and-white. “I’d rather shoot the mess than the clean area, because I grew up in such a messy, grimy house.” 

Since the unintentional inception of this project 10 years ago, Glazzard has progressively traversed into larger cities, from Halifax to Manchester to London. During his second year of university in Manchester, a fixation on documentation emerged as he began capturing his immediate surroundings with diaristic fervour – close friends, lovers, his chosen family. “I sometimes get nervous about it – what if my friends think I’m just obsessed with them?” he half-jokes.

  • Read next: Free-spirited, otherworldly portraits of Mexico City’s queer youth

In the rare instance that Glazzard finds himself without his camera, he takes to notebooks instead, encapsulating the moment in any way he can. Punctuating the hazy, lived-in images throughout the book are photocopied images of his handwritten lists, clearly defined and contrasting, resetting the flow of pages.

One list begins with ‘Things that remind me off home’. Among cig butts, a mouldy washing machine and dirty floorboards, he also writes of warm bed, hot bath and Kate Bush – a favourite of Glazzard’s late mum. “She would go around the house naked, singing Kate Bush,” he says. “I had one thing of my mum’s and it's gone. I can’t have her in the work, and that’s heartbreaking. So to have her in the list is really nice.”

If photography is the ultimate act of preservation, Glazzard has no intention of letting a moment slip past him. In his exploration of archival materials, Glazzard has struggled to find reflections of his history: the British trans experience. Since beginning this project, he’s seen mounting anger and depression throughout the queer community. At the same time, he’s noticed a new craving for visibility from his peers. As he considers whether grief can keep someone alive, his living archive memorialises those closest to him, joy and loss intermingling as he holds on to those who have already parted from his life and those who remain close.

  • Read next: In Birmingham’s punk underground, hardcore is queer

Over the past decade, Glazzard has witnessed and captured the growth of his dearest friends, like Ella, blue-toned and youthful in one image, pregnant-bellied and held by her partner in another, the two standing with eyes turned softly downward. In another image, Glazzard’s best friend Ames reclines against a hospital bed. Pre-surgery, they steal a glance over their freckled shoulder, a strip of gauze pressed to one side. Glazzard’s own transition is traced throughout the book, self-portraits narrating the passage of time in bathroom mirrors or against blank walls, his signature approach. 

“It’s so important that you photograph yourself so that you have the power over your own image,” he says. “Images are put online and then get eaten up. I’ll put them in print or exhibitions because I don’t want them to become a spectacle.” That instinct to protect extends over Glazzard’s self-portraiture and into the friends and lovers who populate his work. Born from lived experience, his photographs resist the polished, commercial language so often imposed on queer bodies, instead safeguarding something more real: people growing up, changing, grieving, and caring for one another. 

After a decade spent trying to hold on to the people around him, Glazzard now finds himself somewhere unexpectedly settled. There is the book he never quite believed he would make, paying the rent he never thought he’d be able to afford each month, and the steady relationships that surround him. “I feel the safest I have ever felt in my life,” he says. For someone so accustomed to preserving what might disappear, there is something quietly radical in having a life that, for once, feels secure.

The Sound of Dirt and Beauty (2026) by Jesse Glazzard published by SPBH Editions / MACK.

items.title: Behind the curtain at Alternative Miss World 1981
items.excerpt: Olympia glamour — Running a subversive take on the traditional beauty pageant, the Andrew Logan organised event prioritised underground creativity and invention. Photographer David Corio went behind the scenes at its biggest edition.
items.content:
Olympia glamour — Running a subversive take on the traditional beauty pageant, the Andrew Logan organised event prioritised underground creativity and invention. Photographer David Corio went behind the scenes at its biggest edition. 

After a visit to the Crufts dog show, artist Andrew Logan was struck by genius. He would apply canine criteria – poise, personality, and originality – to contestants in a beauty pageant unlike any before: Alternative Miss World. In 1972, Logan hosted the first edition at his Hackney studio, setting the underground aflame with subversive notions of glamour, style, and self invention. 

Seizing the moment, Logan staged the 1978 edition, co-hosted by Divine, as the subject of The Alternative Miss World, a 1980 documentary film that premiered at the Cannes Film Festival. Incensed, the Miss World organisation struck back, attempting to block the film’s London debut, which was scheduled the same night at their televised pageant. In a curious twist of fate, future Prime Minister Tony Blair represented the Alternative Miss World organisation in court, with Lord Denning ultimately dismissing the case.  

The following year, Logan came back strong, staging the largest edition in the pageant’s history at the Grand Hall of Olympia on October 2, 1981, and later broadcast on Channel 4. The theme was royalty, and with it came untold decadence. The runway ran long, as did the event, with 35 contestants parading up and down a 250-foot catwalk until three in the morning. Among those in the mix was photographer David Corio, who revisits the unforgettable displays of pomp and circumstance in Alternative Miss World Olympia, London 1981 (Café Royal Books). 

  • Read next: Remembering Taboo, the party that reshaped ’80s London nightlife

“London was really buzzing in 1981,” says Corio, then 21, who was outside most nights photographing concerts and clubs for New Musical Express and THE FACE. “I was shooting anything and everything from music to political demos. It was a time of a lot of experimentation and fashion trends. Bands like Bow Wow Wow were wearing Vivienne Westwood and every week seemed to bring another act that was going to be the next big thing.” 

Corio remembers mid-century beauty pageants as “a very odd scene” despite their popularity among the mainstream. “Seeing white women with large hair in swimsuits and high heels being interviewed about world affairs and what they would do to improve the world was just plain weird!” he remembers. 

But Alternative Miss World offered a reprieve, embracing the carnivalesque possibilities of glamour gone wild. French singer Hermine Demoriane and Miss Dinosaur make a delightful pair, reminding women when in doubt to choose the bear. Fashion designer Zandra Rhodes and New Romantic visionary Steve Strange kiki in the front row, while stylist Judy Blame carries on backstage.  

  • Read next: A life in colour: Capturing the punks of 1980s Britain

Given free reign to shoot anywhere he liked, Corio naturally gravitated to the backstage scene. Amidst the mayhem, the competitors soldiered on, going through multiple costume changes and an interview with Logan. “There was a general sense of panic and disorganisation, which is probably the case at a lot of fashion shows. It was chaotic on the stage as well with the dinosaur falling over, rollerskaters crashing into other contestants,” Corio says. “The whole evening was general mayhem really – that much I do remember – in a nice way of course!”

Alternative Miss World Olympia, London 1981 by David Corio is published by Café Royal Books.

items.title: New exhibition highlights British radical living over 200 years
items.excerpt: Earthly Paradise — Taking place at the William Morris Gallery, it explores the homes and lives of artists, writers, musicians and more, as well as the conditions that allowed them to thrive. A new exhibition coming to
items.content:
Earthly Paradise — Taking place at the William Morris Gallery, it explores the homes and lives of artists, writers, musicians and more, as well as the conditions that allowed them to thrive.

A new exhibition coming to London will explore the radical people and places that have shaped contemporary Britain.

On view at the William Morris Gallery in Walthamstow between October 3, 2026 and March 28, 2027, Earthly Paradise: Radical Living in the UK, dives into the communities and conditions that have allowed art and activism to thrive over the past 200 years.

It focuses on the living spaces and homes that people living outside of mainstream society have occupied, including squats, communes and anti-racist housing movements that encourage alternative ways of thinking and existing.

  • Read next: Sepia splashed memories of Britain’s ’90s squatting and free party scene

The exhibition will feature photographs, objects, paintings, drawings and sound archives, featuring ephemera and work from the likes of Oscar Wilde, Lee Miller, Sunil Gupta and Martin Parr.

Through its themes and the works on show, the exhibition will raise questions about money and class within capitalism, and who has access to create and rebel. Photography from the 1990s onwards explores how rising rents and house prices, in the wake of the 1980 Right to Buy scheme introduced by Margaret Thatcher’s Conservative government, has changed our relationship with homes and the ability to create and think differently.

Earthly Paradise: Radical Living in the UK is part of Art Fund’s ‘Going Places’ touring exhibitions programme, which sees museums across the UK collaborate in sharing their collections with different local communities. It has been developed with Tŷ Pawb in Wrexham, Blackwell – The Arts & Crafts House in Bowness-on-Windermere and Dovecot Studios in Edinburgh.

  • Read next: Remembering the radical anti-nuclear Greenham Women’s Peace Camp
The exhbition is curated by Hadrian Garrard, Director of William Morris Gallery; Linsey Young, independent curator; and Tayyabah Tahir, Assistant Curator at William Morris Gallery. Garrard said: “William Morris was in an open marriage and wanted to completely blur the lines between domestic life and making and experiencing art. 

“He was friends with gay men and women, anarchists and revolutionaries – and he lived radically in the ways that we see many other artists live through history,” he continued. “This show looks at how the home has acted as a site for challenging societal norms – what that has meant through history and what the possibilities are for this in today’s world.”

Earthly Paradise: Radical Living in the UK is curated by Hadrian Garrard, Director of William Morris Gallery; Linsey Young, independent curator; and Tayyabah Tahir, Assistant Curator at William Morris Gallery.

Earthly Paradise: Radical Living in the UK is on view at William Morris Gallery between October 3, 2026 and March 28, 2027.

items.title: What life on the Strait of Hormuz is really like
items.excerpt: Southern Winds — Bandar Abbas based photographer Morteza Niknahad has been capturing the diverse communities and stories of his local region since he first picked up a camera. His new series highlights the human impact of war.
items.content:
Southern Winds — Bandar Abbas based photographer Morteza Niknahad has been capturing the diverse communities and stories of his local region since he first picked up a camera. His new series highlights the human impact of war.

On February 28, 2026, Iran announced that it was closing the Strait of Hormuz. Earlier that day, the USA launched a swathe of air strikes against the country under ‘Operation Epic Fury’ including one that killed the country’s supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who had ruled over the nation since 1989. Despite President Donald Trump telling US lawmakers that the war “would take approximately four to six weeks”, attacks continue to rumble on, with four people killed at a wedding celebration after a US missile hit a house in southern Iran on Tuesday, September 1, according to the Iranian Red Crescent.

But its closing also placed a small, previously largely overlooked waterway between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman directly into the international consciousness. At 104 miles long, the Strait is a maritime pinchpoint that connects the Persian Gulf to the rest of the world’s oceans. It’s a crucial stretch in the global shipping trade, with roughly a quarter of the world’s seaborne oil travelling through the Strait and a third of its fertiliser. Prices for fuel, food and more have risen across the world as supply has tightened, while a global food crisis is predicted later in the year as a lack of nitrogen fertilisers are likely to heavily disrupt harvests and crop cycles. 

Photographer Morteza Niknahad grew up in Bandar Abbas – a coastal city in southern Iran, situated on the north shore of the Strait of Hormuz. As a young child, he nearly died in the sea, which led to an understanding and respect of the water’s power. “I remember drowning in the Persian Gulf, but fortunately my father managed to save me,” Niknahad remembers. “A deep fear took root in me that later transformed into a meaningful relationship with the sea.”

  • Read next: A melancholic portrait of youth, rebellion and womanhood in Iran

He’s watched it switch suddenly overnight from a rather nondescript strait to globalisation’s breaking point. “During my childhood, the Strait of Hormuz was simply an international waterway and held no other meaning for us. As a teenager, I would sometimes go to the seashore at night hoping to see a mermaid,” he says. “But after the recent tensions, its definition and meaning have changed.”

It was as a teenager when he first picked up a camera and began documenting the world and people around him. Focusing on the diverse communities and people of the Strait of Hormuz, his photographs explore the unique shape of life in the region, crafted by the constant flow of water, people and goods across centuries. In an area that has been key in trade and movement long before the creation of the United States and Israel, borders mean little to those who live on its coast.

“The culture of southern Iran is very different and diverse,” he explains. “The people of this region are very warm and generous. I believe we have taken this quality, in part, from the sea. At the same time, the presence of the sea throughout history has allowed us to be in contact with the world, and the world around us.”

  • Read next: In photos: Lebanon’s women against a backdrop of war

Niknahad’s new series, Southern Winds, combines his deep archive of the area with photographs taken since February 28. With the beginning of strikes and war, the Iranian government introduced sweeping restrictions, including over movement and access to the internet. As a result, he began taking pictures using his phone camera, rather than his usual analogue setup. Recent shots show people standing by the seaside, or on rooftops as black smoke billows from the distance. He explains that as the sea has become unsafe, fishermen have stopped going out to catch food, while maritime trade has stopped, drastically affecting the local economy.

“I only took the wartime photographs with a mobile phone, because it was not possible to photograph with a camera unless you were a photographer with official permits,” he says. “What made me leave the house was seeing something new and bitter. Ships burning at sea and the sky over the city turning black with smoke. I thought I had to document these historic moments so I could look back at them later and tell their story.”

Alongside these, Niknahad lays out old family portraits, as well as studio portraits of those who lived around the Strait of Hormuz’s islands – both as an exploration of his memory and roots in the area, but also highlighting how people’s lives and stories have always existed in the area. There’s photographs of local cultures and rituals, including the Zar healing ritual ceremony to groups of women riding around on motorcycles, as well as people of African descent who have lived there for generations.

  • Read next: The global skateboarding crew reshaping Muslim sisterhood

“Seeing the people who live by the shore and hearing their stories has always been sweet and instructive for me,” Niknahad says. “I think these people are very oppressed and voiceless. The media usually pays attention to headlines and news events, not necessarily to the lives of the people behind those headlines. As a result, I have always felt that I must tell the story. Every moment of this path of discovery is memorable for me.”

His work helps shine a different light on an area that is rarely understood beyond its strategic importance on the world’s geopolitical chessboard, while shining a light on the real impacts felt by people in the region as a result of the war started by the USA and Israel. But Niknahad is quick to remind that the region is no stranger to conflict, and its people will continue on existing in the area long into the future.

“Different generations come and go, but there are common chapters in their experiences, that we too have experienced in the last hundred years,” he says. “People know that this story has no clear final chapter. They are getting by with difficulty and continuing to live because they have no other choice.”

  • Read next: Eerie, strangely evocative photos of container ships at sea

To see more of Morteza Niknahad’s work, follow him on Instagram.

items.title: Nick Haymes’s intimate portrait of his family’s life
items.excerpt: Chronograph — Over 25 years, the photographer documented his son’s lives as they grew into adults. The resulting photobook is an exploration of the passage of time, as well as the optimism of youth. Photographer Nick H
items.content:
Chronograph — Over 25 years, the photographer documented his son’s lives as they grew into adults. The resulting photobook is an exploration of the passage of time, as well as the optimism of youth.

Photographer Nick Haymes’s newest book, Chronograph (SPBH Editions), opens on September 11 just moments after the North Tower was hit, the crystal blue sky slowly filling with ominous clouds of smoke. “That was the end of the 21st century before it even began,” he says.

Realising life is short, Haymes and his partner Lina began their life with her young son, Philipp, and soon welcomed Lawrence, a boy of their own, into the family. As a stay at home father, Haymes lived by Dad Code. “I never spoke to them as kids,” he says. “They’re always spoken to as adults, and then we figured it out. I’m not one of those parents who follow them down a slide. If they’re going to go break their nose, they can. You do it once, and then you never do it again.” 

His “live and let live” ethos created space for self discovery at every age, the every day moments of his children’s lives evoking the freewheeling spirit of Pee-wee’s Playhouse. “Everyone becomes extended family and ends up in our house at some point so there is always a crossover,” says Haymes, who has introduced his children to muses like Love Bailey and Gabe, who have inspired his previous monographs.  

  • Read next: An unconventional portrait of queer motherhood

Haymes’s love for the next generation lies at the core of his work. “I photograph youth culture because there’s something intrinsically fantastic about it,” he says. “There is an optimism that at some point you lose. It’s like, oh my God, the world is falling apart, what are we going to do? But at some point you’ll listen to a 20-year-old, and think, maybe you’re right, maybe it can change, and why not? It’s good to hear.” 

With Chronograph, Haymes devoted a quarter of a century to photographing his family, allowing the story to unfold at the natural pace of life, while his publisher Bruno Ceschel waited patiently for 15 years until the story was complete. Bookended by death – collective and personal – Haymes reimagines the domestic narrative through the lens of fatherhood, a vantage point unexplored despite the preponderance of men across all disciplines of the photo industry.  

For the better part of photography history, the domestic interior has been largely disregarded as a serious space, in no small part due to the fact it has been dominated by women artists such as Sally Mann, Tina Barney, Melonie Bennett, Judith Black, and Susan Kandel. But in more recent years, institutions have finally embraced what visionaries have always known: our first, most profound experience of photography is the family photo album. Here we discover ourselves and loved ones cast against the backdrop of ancestry and lineage cast among snapshots of moments both grand and intimate.

  • Read next: Motoyuki Daifu’s chaotic vision of the Japanese family home

“This isn’t a book on parenthood. It’s more a book about existence, understanding, and appreciating the time you have on the planet and how you spend it.” Haymes says. “If you’re going to have kids, you may as well be active in their lives in some form. I never wanted to censor them. Same as that, I never used a pacifier; I think that’s just wrong because for the rest of your whole life, you’re told to shut up and get in line.”

Chronograph (2026) by Nick Haymes published by SPBH Editions / MACK.

items.title: Kristina Rozhkova’s scatty, confronting portrait of captivity
items.excerpt: Gut Feeling — The Russian artist’s 2024 arrest and subsequent detention opened her eye towards the omnipresent dynamics of power and control. Her new photobook is a stark exploration of being trapped. On June 19, 2024,
items.content:
Gut Feeling — The Russian artist’s 2024 arrest and subsequent detention opened her eye towards the omnipresent dynamics of power and control. Her new photobook is a stark exploration of being trapped.

On June 19, 2024, Kristina Rozhkova was arrested in Russia alongside three others – Anna Panteleeva, Yaroslava Guminaya, and Sergey Evstyukhin. First, they were taken to a temporary detention centre (IVS), before Rozhkova was transferred to a pre-trial detention (SIZO) facility for two months. For the next year and a half, she had to attend “endless” court hearings.

It came after a photoshoot they had organised in a Russian Orthodox cemetery. “There were no victims, no damaged property and no physical evidence,” she says. “It featured elements of shibari [Japanese rope bondage], which was a technique I frequently incorporated into my work. We wore structured outfits, and the focus was entirely aesthetic rather than overtly political – there was nothing vulgar or inherently provocative.”

But Rozhkova claims that the group were the targets of a co-ordinated attack from a group known as Muzhskoye Gosudarstvo, which translates to ‘Male State’, who reported them to the authorities, even though none of the final photographs had been published. It came after one of the models in the shoot had publicly called out a male artist for sexual assault prior to the shoot.

  • Read next: In a world of noise, IC3PEAK are finding radicality in the quiet

The only thing that had surfaced in public was a leaked screenshot of a behind the scenes video. “It was terrible. Being in SIZO at first was completely unbearable – those two months were genuinely agonizing,” she recalls. “My cellmates used to tell me that the first two months are always the hardest period to survive, and after that, it gradually becomes easier to manage month by month.”

House arrest was hardly easier. “At first, house arrest felt like absolute paradise – you sleep in a normal bed, watch movies, read and focus on hobbies,” she continues. “But after two months, I realised it was its own form of hell. I couldn’t go for a walk or step outside, and I had to watch my life pass me by without understanding why.”

That period, which ultimately consumed two years of her life, without considering the long-term mental effects since, inspired her to create her series and newly published photobook Gut Feeling. Its photographs – which are scatty, disquieting and occasionally even violent – explore the physical experience of being trapped with no control or way out. Photos with chains and ropes are sequenced alongside people physically holding others down – one shot sees a person squatting, with their feet obscuring a man’s face.

  • Read next: Tender, carefree portraits of young Ukrainians before the war

Animals also play a key theme in the book. There are mice in jars, a goose being restrained, and references to horses and dogs throughout. Growing up, Rozhkova was surrounded by them – her mother was a dog breeder, and she regularly attended dog shows. Her first friend was a bull terrier, and she described her childhood as Mowgli-like. Her arrest brought back many of those memories and sharpened her focus on the relationship between animals and humans.

“Being confined created a very specific physical and psychological feeling – one I later tried to recreate in my work – of being a trapped animal in a tiny cage,” Rozhkova explains. “Imagine putting vastly different species into one tight space. If you keep animals of the same kind together under proper conditions, they might get along, like getting a second dog so the first one isn’t lonely. But SIZO was a forced mixing of completely incompatible human lives in atrocious conditions. The environment was so wretched that everyone became overwhelmed by aggression, rage and sickness. It was utterly inhumane.”

Yet Rozhkova’s arrest didn’t come in isolation. The past decade and a half have seen the Russian authorities increasingly clamp down on dissenting voices and artists in particular – notably beginning with the arrest of punk group Pussy Riot in 2012, but intensifying in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. According to Human Rights Watch, as of July 2026, there were 1,715 political prisoners in the country, which was up by 997 from a year before.

  • Read next: Analogue Appreciation: Maria Teriaeva’s five pieces that remind her of home

“Before COVID-19, things in the country felt relatively normal – neither I nor my circle felt any heavy pressure,” she says. “The turning point came after the pandemic, but the real nightmare began when the full-scale war started. From then on, literally with every passing month and day, the circle was tightening faster and faster. Authorities started raiding art exhibitions, closing entire museums and controlling art fairs to remove specific works. It became glaringly obvious how impossible it was for artists to truly express themselves.”

The photographs ultimately speak to more than just her arrest, but the array of power dynamics that dominate human existence on earth. Whether it’s parents with their children, husbands and wives, rich and poor, governments with populations, people and pets, or the livestock industry at large, there are structural imbalances that govern our everyday lives.

“I see the project as universal. It can be interpreted through everyday, intimate, sexual or deeply personal lenses,” she says. “Totalitarian frameworks and mechanics of control exist everywhere – within medical institutions, schools and universities.”

  • Read next: In photos: Inmates of the oldest women’s prison in the USA

Like many other young, creative people of her generation, Rozhkova now lives outside of Russia. Around 1,000,000 people are believed to have emigrated since February 2022, mostly under the age of 45. Yet while she hopes the future holds an end to the war and a free Russia, her life has been changed forever.

“Before I was arrested, I could never have imagined that something like this would happen to me, or how brutal the reality of it is,” she continues. “Once you’ve been through it, you can no longer trust the world in the same way. It fundamentally shatters your trust in society, in authorities, and in safety itself.”

Gut Feeling by Kristina Rozhkova is published by VOID.

items.title: Shawn Walker’s layered, psychedelic vision of Harlem’s streets
items.excerpt: From BeBop to Illusion — Using glass as a means to illuminate the city’s different layers, the longtime photographer and filmmaker is publishing his first monograph at the age of 86. For photographer Shawn Walker, life
items.content:
From BeBop to Illusion — Using glass as a means to illuminate the city’s different layers, the longtime photographer and filmmaker is publishing his first monograph at the age of 86.

For photographer Shawn Walker, life is not black and white but a symphony of textures and tones, layered like the rhythms, harmonies, and melodies of his hometown. Born in Harlem in 1940, Walker got his start accompanying his uncle, Herbert Hoover, a bar photographer who became one of the first in the neighbourhood to get a Polaroid. By the late ’50s, he was hanging out in storied jazz clubs like Minton’s Playhouse and Birdland, while practicing his own instrument: the camera. 

Watching his uncle’s thriving side hustle, Walker intuitively understood he could make photographs without having to rely on it as his livelihood. He joined a local photography group that merged with another in 1963 to become Kamoinge, today the oldest nonprofit photography collective in the world. Walker, the youngest founding member, was joined by luminaries including Roy DeCarava, Adger Cowans, Anthony Barboza, and later Ming Smith and Frank Stewart. 

It was here, in Kamoinge members’ homes during their spirited Sunday sessions, that Walker learned photography was not just a trade, it was an art. There were no rules, other than he could write his own, and so he did, devoting a lifetime to elevating photography to the realm of fine art.In 2019, Walker became the first Black photographer to have his archive acquired by the Library of Congress, his collection of over 100,000 images housed alongside luminaries including Toni Morrison, James Baldwin, and Maya Angelou – all of whom he has photographed during his storied seven-decade career. 

  • Read next: Sombre, tender photos of final goodbyes during the Harlem Renaissance

But Walker refuses to rest on the laurels of his success, preferring to blaze his own path as a visionary iconoclast. In recent months, his 1970s photograph of a masked man blowing bubbles in Central Park was on view in Sixties Surreal at the Whitney Museum of American Art, taking his rightful place alongside contemporaries like Diane Arbus, Andy Warhol, and Lee Friedlander. “As a Black artist, what we’re supposed to do is move Black art to another level. We’re not here just to repeat [ourselves or someone else],” Walker says. 

Now in his 86th year, Walker introduces his very first monograph, From BeBop to Illusion (Kurt Boone Books), a hypnotic chronicle of New York City through a reflective eye. Drawing inspiration from DeCarava, M.C. Escher, and Henri Cartier-Bresson, Walker takes to the streets of his hometown, turning the camera away from passersby, choosing to go through the looking glass instead. He takes aim at vast expanses of glass windows soaring up to the sky, these delectable jewel boxes of luxury commerce dazzling the eye. 

Everywhere it is mannequins dressed within an inch of their lives, done up in finery as they loom above the pavement, looking down on pedestrians shuttling about their lives. Walker situates them in the landscape of illusion, fashion, and fantasy. But as the rhythm picks up, it slides into a nightmare: skulls appear, bulging eyes and rotting teeth. The end of the earth is upon us; soon we will go the way of the dinosaur whose monstrous jaws are the unironic centrepiece of a Christmas window display. 

  • Read next: Vintage portraits of Harlem street style

The ever-present spectre of annihilation, be it by the forces of nature or the hand of the state, reveals itself in the silence between notes, where the theme of jazz becomes a departure point for something far more disconcerting. “Are you familiar with the neutron bomb?” Walker asks of the now-banned thermonuclear weapons program developed by the United States in the 1950s and ’60s, designed for maximum death while leaving the environment fully intact. 

“It struck me that somebody decided to make a bomb that killed people but did not destroy infrastructure; that just blew me away,” Walker continues. It brought back childhood memories of The World, the Flesh and the Devil, the 1959 film starring Harry Belafonte as a post-apocalyptic survivor who travels to New York in search of others. In those haunting scenes of emptiness populated only by inanimate mannequins, Walker recognised the presence of parallel universes that reveal themselves through the cracks of light where this work was born.

“I don’t feel I am supposed to stand still in my career,” Walker says. “I was put here for a purpose.” 

From BeBop to Illusion by Shawn Walker is published by Kurt Boone Books.
